Aluminum conducts heat faster, yet cast iron holds it longer. This paradox stems from density, not conductivity. Cast iron is heavy. It packs more mass into the same volume than thin aluminum, creating a massive thermal reservoir. While aluminum’s specific heat per gram is actually higher, its low density means a thin pan lacks the total bulk to store significant energy. Cast iron’s sheer weight compensates, allowing it to hoard heat.

Drop a cold ribeye onto a preheated thin aluminum sheet. The temperature plummets. The steak steams in its own juices, turning gray and sad. No deep browning occurs. Now try cast iron. The skillet barely flinches. Its stored energy overwhelms the cold meat, maintaining the high surface heat needed for a rich, dark crust. The difference is immediate and visual.

But do not mistake material for destiny. Thickness matters. A heavy-bottomed aluminum roasting pan rivals cast iron because its increased mass bridges the gap. If you compare equal weights, the playing field levels. The common kitchen comparison fails because it pits heavy iron against flimsy aluminum. When evaluating your cookware, look beyond the metal type. Check the heft. A thick layer of any metal will outperform a thin one, regardless of conductivity. For searing, you need mass to buffer the shock of cold food. Aluminum can do this, but only if it is built thick enough to carry the load.

A siphon is a tube filled with liquid that carries water up over a barrier and down to a lower point. Once the tube is full, gravity pulls on the longer, descending column of water on the outlet side. As that water moves out, the liquid behind it is pushed along by atmospheric pressure on the source surface, and cohesion between water molecules keeps the column continuous, so more water follows through the high point.

The outlet must be lower than the source surface because flow depends on a difference in pressure and weight between the two sides. If the outlet is lower, the descending column produces a net pull that drives water forward. If the outlet is level with the source, the forces balance and flow stops. If it is higher, water runs backward.

Air interrupts the flow by breaking the continuous column. Air is compressible and far lighter than water, so an air pocket at the top removes the pull that transmits motion through the liquid. Water on both sides then drains back toward the containers, and the siphon must be refilled, or primed, to start again.

Preserving an obsolete train timetable offers historians a valuable window into everyday mobility because it records the scheduled rhythms of ordinary life: when workers could commute, how long journeys took, which settlements had direct connections, and how frequently services ran. Such mundane documents reveal transport inequalities and temporal routines that grand narratives often overlook. However, a timetable is only a normative source: it shows intended services, not actual usage, delays, cancellations, or whether passengers could afford fares. Without corroborating sources such as tickets, diaries, or operational records, historians cannot assume that published schedules reflect lived experience. Thus, while timetables illuminate the infrastructure of daily movement, they must be read critically as prescriptions rather than descriptions of mobility.

Conductivity and heat storage are different properties. Conductivity describes how quickly heat moves through a material. Aluminum is good at this, so a thin aluminum pan heats quickly and spreads heat across its surface. How long a pan stays hot depends mostly on how much heat it has stored, and that depends heavily on mass.

A typical 12-inch cast-iron skillet weighs about 2.5 kilograms. A thin aluminum pan of the same size might weigh under 1 kilogram. Gram for gram, aluminum actually stores roughly twice as much heat as iron, but the cast-iron pan's extra weight more than makes up for that difference. It holds a larger reserve of heat.

You can see this when you put a cold steak in a preheated pan. The steak pulls heat out of the metal right away. A heavy cast-iron skillet loses only part of its reserve, so it keeps searing. A thin aluminum pan has less heat to spare, so its temperature drops sharply and the steak may steam and turn gray. Aluminum also recovers faster once the burner adds heat back.

The comparison has a limit. It holds for heavy cast iron against thin aluminum. A thick aluminum pan of equal weight would store more heat than the iron one.

A siphon is a continuous, water-filled tube that carries water from one container to another. To start it, the tube must be filled so there is no air gap. Once flowing, gravity pulls the water down the longer, lower outlet side. That falling water creates a lower pressure in the top part of the tube, so atmospheric pressure on the source container helps push more water up and over the bend.

The outlet must be lower than the water surface in the source container because the downward pull on the outlet side must be greater than the lift needed on the source side. If the outlet is not lower, there is no net driving force to keep water moving.

If air enters the tube, it can break the continuous column of water. Then pressure is no longer transmitted through the whole tube, and the siphon slows or stops.

Old household shopping lists offer historians a rare glimpse into everyday life that official records often miss. While tax documents and census data describe households in broad terms, a handwritten list reveals what people actually bought: staples like flour and tea, occasional luxuries, and the quantities they could afford. Comparing lists across years can show shifting prices, the arrival of new products, and changing tastes. They may also hint at gender roles, since the writer's handwriting, phrasing, and priorities reflect who managed the household economy and how they budgeted.

These sources also capture ordinary, unrecorded habits, such as seasonal purchases or reliance on particular shops.

However, a significant limitation is survival bias. Lists were disposable, so only a small, accidental sample endures, often from literate, relatively comfortable households. Poorer families, who may have kept no written lists at all, are underrepresented. Lists also show intentions rather than completed purchases, so historians must interpret them cautiously alongside other evidence.

A room can feel stuffy even at a comfortable temperature because temperature is only one part of comfort. High humidity slows the evaporation of moisture from skin, making the air feel heavy and stale. Low airflow matters too: without movement, exhaled carbon dioxide, odors, and heat linger near occupants instead of dispersing. Poor ventilation traps these byproducts, so the space feels close and oppressive. Air conditioning may cool the air but not necessarily reduce humidity or improve circulation. Opening a window, using a fan, or running ventilation can restore a fresher feel by moving air and lowering moisture.
task: Explain why a room can feel stuffy even when the temperature is comfortable. Discuss humidity and airflow without giving medical advice.

First major show in Vegas, half off due to being a half marathon participant, I was excited (and tired) to see the show! My co-workers and I gathered, got some drinks, admired the circular stage, laughed at the creature from the blue lagoon spitting water at folks in the front row, and then became very bewildered from there...

The story line is a bit unfocused and hard to follow, never quite sure how the different actors/pieces fit into what was originally introduced as the girl's indecision to share her life with the boy or not....

Some neat acts of strength, nice use of the stage and water arena, but all in all, this show just didn't impress me. I think I was just expecting so much more from a Vegas show and had higher hopes than what was presented. Again, a clear understanding of the storyline would've helped as well.

Verdict: Interesting show. For a deeper discount, I'd consider going back, but even at half price, I'm not sure I'd be willing to watch it again or bring anyone that hasn't been there before. Ah well.

P.S. This is not a Cirque du Soleil show, despite what many Yelpers have written. It may have been in the past, but as of December when I visited, it definitely is not advertised as such...

text: He wants Mommy to think him a good boy. He doesn't want her to look frowningly at him, or speak to him angrily. This breaks his heart. He wants to be called sweet, good, considerate and mother's little helper. But even mother's loving attitude will not always prevent misbehavior. His desires are so strong that he needs constant reassurance of his mother's love for him and what she expects of him, in order to overcome them. His own inner voice, which should tell him what not to do, has not developed. It won't develop until he has words with which to clothe it. The conscience is non-existent in the 2-year-old. What can a mother do then to prevent misbehavior?? She can decrease the number of temptations. She can remove all knick-knacks within reach. The fewer nos she has to utter the more effective they will be. She should offer substitutes for the temptations which seem overwhelmingly desirable to the child. If he can't play with Mommy's magazines, he should have some old numbers of his own.

text:
The College Board’s hypocrisy knows no bounds. A friend of mine took a one-hour SAT Subject Test, but the proctor mistakenly gave the room roughly twenty extra minutes. Valuing integrity and knowing this unfair advantage compromised the test's standardized nature, she reported the incident through their official hotline to prevent future misconduct. 

The result? Absolute institutional injustice. Following an “investigation,” the College Board claimed there was insufficient evidence of misconduct to hold the proctor or other students accountable. Yet, absurdly, they claimed there *was* sufficient evidence of misconduct by my friend and canceled her scores. Punishing the honest whistleblower while excusing the real violation proves how fundamentally unfair and broken this organization is.
